comments.text: I'm sorry, but I think you got this one mostly wrong. I use AI quite a bit, too, because I want to know what it's capable of, and because it saves me time here and there. Flight automation makes pilots more powerful, because it helps them leverage their intelligence to *just* the personal and/or safety risk situations that are so rare, but matter so much. AI is not like that. I find that AI makes my intelligence obsolete. A lower level of capability may have not: the ability to generate short snippets of code, to return only answers to rather concise questions. Sadly, even Claude Sonnet (yes, Sonnet) is already capable of reading my published papers on partial differential equations and reverse-engineering my entire unpublished codebase. I am a young researcher. In the past, that code would have been my intellectual capital. Someone would have had to spend months or years to reproduce it in full. Or, much more easily, just hire me. Now it can be done in hours, no contact necessary. A technology that takes care of the drudgery and makes space for "top of the pyramid" work IS good. It's empowering. The video's best historical examples show AI automating tasks within jobs while humans expand into higher value work. But every example given...ATMs, spreadsheets, word processors... automated a narrow, specific task while leaving the broader cognitive role intact for humans to grow into. The elevator operator, the video's one case of complete elimination, was eliminated precisely because there was no broader cognitive role to expand into. Most routine knowledge work today looks more like the elevator operator than the airline pilot. Narrow, well defined, with limited room to expand which is exactly why this transition may not follow the historical augmentation pattern. There is no historical predicant tied to AI

The "elevator operator" argument severely oversimplifies both history and what is happening right now in tech. Mechanization didn't just transform jobs; it wiped out entire categories, from switchboard operators and typesetters to over 38% of the agricultural workforce. The transition wasn't seamless; it was decades of painful structural displacement. We are already seeing this exact play out with software developers today. Companies aren't always running loud mass layoffs; they're using silent displacement, junior dev hiring freezes, non-backfills after resignations, and compressing 10-person engineering teams down to 3 or 4 using tools like Claude and Cursor. Industrial automation replaced physical muscle in narrow tasks over generations. Generative AI replaces general cognitive labor across hundreds of white-collar fields simultaneously. Treating 21st-century AI like 20th-century push-button elevators isn't economic insight... it's head-in-the-sand analysis. My opinion is that you did not do your homework here.
